meta.title: Did the Midterms Destroy All Hope for Data Centers? | E2360
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · local data-center bans and the market dip · Calacanis's midterm scorecard · lab community pledges · AI copyright licensing · AI token budgets and Apple · tax risk after the midterms

snapshot: Democrats took the House and Senate; many ran against data centers, and over a dozen Ohio towns plus places in Kansas, Florida and California voted to halt or restrict them.
Texas, Georgia and Ohio hold more than **40%** of planned US data-center capacity; OpenAI leaders reportedly discussed resetting next year's capacity expectations.
Calacanis calls the tech sell-off (5-6% in a day) **overblown** and a generational buy-the-dip moment; he expects Democrats to settle on a deal where data centers pay taxes, power and water costs.
OpenAI published new community commitments two days after the vote; Calacanis says leadership means repeating the message, and that data centers should be depoliticized.
Anthropic signed its first publisher licensing deal (AP, election coverage); Calacanis calls real-time use of news content not fair use and floats paying 3% of revenue to content owners.
Apple is cutting daily AI spend caps for engineers; Calacanis expects corporate AI seats to settle at **$100-300 per month** and sees Apple as the late, local-hardware winner.
Post-election tax fear: Calacanis expects New York and California to hit 60% and says he would retire at that rate; he proposes taxing margin loans above $10M.

themes.title: Voters restrict data centers; Calacanis says the sell-off is a buying chance
themes.lead: Local bans and a Texas governor-elect's pause hit the data-center trade, but Calacanis expects a deal where builders pay their way.
bullets: Lon Harris: Democrats won both chambers, many on slowing AI and data centers; **over a dozen Ohio towns** voted to halt or restrict development, with similar bans in Kansas, Florida and California.
Texas' governor-elect campaigned on pausing construction until new regulation (per the Wall Street Journal); Texas, Georgia and Ohio hold **40%+** of planned capacity.
By Wednesday senior OpenAI leaders were discussing whether to reset next year's capacity expectations; Bloomberg says Microsoft is souring on neoclouds such as nscale and Iren.
Calacanis: tech fell **5-6%** in a day after a rally the morning after the vote, and he says a slowed AI trade could mean a two-to-four-year recession that is blamed on Democrats.

He cites Gavin Baker: Texas laws for data centers delivering in 2028-29 would require taxes, no power-price increase, no water impact, union labor and a seat for Texans; Calacanis calls it a reasonable middle ground.
He says it is a good moment to nibble on Nvidia, Amazon, Uber, Tesla and SpaceX, and notes he predicted this post-election peace on the Aug 31 episode (E2332).

themes.title: Reading the midterms: Iran war, cost of living and corruption beat data centers
themes.lead: Harris and Calacanis review the host's earlier Trump calls and say the vote was driven by affordability, the war and perceived corruption, with AI close behind.
bullets: Harris reads exit polls: the **Iran war** first, data centers high, then a perception of corruption; Calacanis adds **cost of living** and affordability.
Calacanis gives Trump an **A to A-plus** on supporting AI and data centers, and says gridlock is the preferred case; he thinks Trump made data centers a wedge issue.

Clips replayed: the Feb 18 2025 take that Trump shouldn't have launched meme coins; the May 14 2025 view that tariffs were chaotic though right in principle; the May 3 2026 view that AI and jobs split the GOP (Bannon, Fuentes, Tucker, Megyn Kelly).
He blames sycophants for tariff chaos, says tariff opponents were brigaded, and cites a Trump-supporting founder's firsthand account as his source.
Calacanis thinks the new Democrats are mostly moderates and will move to the center; Harris says their message was affordability, no corruption and no wars.
Both say Democrats laid low for two years (0 for 4 branches) and let Trump hurt himself; Calacanis would back whoever is president and would invite tech CEOs to DC.

Harris says a winning Democrat (Tlaib Frico, a Texas winner) praised Elon Musk and Ted Cruz the day after, despite Musk spending **$200 million** against him; memes now joke that Zuckerberg and other CEOs, as Reed Hastings predicted, flip back to blue.
Calacanis dismisses Governor Abbott's data-center pause as appeasing voters who hate AI after Dario Amodei's job-loss warnings, and expects the Aug 31 prediction to hold.

quote.text: I think the Democrats are not socialist lunatics in large part

themes.watch: Calacanis presents this as his own record and is the one grading it; he says he declined pressure to join the administration.

themes.title: OpenAI publishes community pledges; Calacanis says repeat them and depoliticize
themes.lead: OpenAI commits to pay full power costs and publish plans, and the host argues the answer to backlash is relentless repetition.
bullets: OpenAI will pay the **full cost of powering** its data centers, seek community input, publish construction plans and **avoid NDAs** with public officials, and urges lawmakers to turn this into law.
Meta, Microsoft, Google and Anthropic have outlined similar commitments; OpenAI told investors in February it targets **$600 billion** in compute spend by 2030.
Calacanis: nothing revolutionary, but leadership is repeating the same line; he gives the example of comparing a data center's water use to a golf course, with seven golf courses locally.
Both argue data centers are not inherently partisan (a Walmart is a more progressive target), and Harris notes cities have long subsidized big-box retail.
themes.watch: Calacanis, an investor in AI, is arguing the industry's case; OpenAI's commitments apply only to centers it owns and operates.

names.name: OpenAI
names.blurb: Published community commitments and a policy blueprint on Nov 5.

themes.title: Anthropic's first licensing deal exposes the unsettled AI copyright map
themes.lead: Anthropic signed with the Associated Press for election coverage; Calacanis lays out four copyright exposures and says two are still open.
bullets: Adweek: Anthropic's first publisher deal, with the **AP** for election coverage, signed just before the midterms; terms undisclosed; OpenAI has more than a dozen (Axel Springer, News Corp, The Atlantic).

Calacanis' four issues: using stolen content (Anthropic's **billion-dollar** pirated-books settlement), breaking terms of service (OpenAI, Greg Brockman's paywall comment), training on content, and outputting others' IP.
He says the first two are cleaned up, training is murky but will go to content companies, and that real-time use of news is **not fair use**.
His fix: give 3% of revenue (about $3 billion a year at a $100 billion run rate) to content owners; Substack would pass 90% through to writers.
themes.watch: These are Calacanis' own legal views as an investor and publisher, not court rulings; the OpenAI vs. New York Times case is pending.

names.name: Anthropic
names.blurb: First licensing deal with the AP; IPO timing is raised as a motive.

themes.title: Apple cuts engineer AI spend caps; Calacanis sees corporate seats rising to $100-300 a month
themes.lead: Apple lowered engineers' daily AI budget from $300 to $200, and the host reads that as proof the all-you-can-eat plan era is ending.
bullets: Bloomberg: Apple cut its daily AI spend cap for engineering teams from **$300 to $200** in October, with some going to **$100** and a $25 limit weighed outside engineering.
Calacanis' team pays about **$40 a month** per head, burning perhaps $2,000 a year in tokens; he expects the minimum corporate price to rise to $100-300 a month ($3-5k a year).
He says Apple will come in last but best, with the best local hardware (and a possible $20,000 Mac Studio for everyone), and that Nvidia and Windows with Microsoft are working on the same.
Harris agrees a model-agnostic Apple platform makes sense, and they price a top-spec Apple desktop at $14,549.

names.blurb: Cutting AI spend caps; Calacanis says it may win late with local hardware.

themes.title: Calacanis fears 60% state tax rates and proposes taxing large margin loans
themes.lead: He expects the next fight to shift from income to assets and says the borrow-against-stock loophole is the easy target.
bullets: Calacanis: if taxes become **60%** he would retire; he expects New York and California to reach 60%, and says the failed billionaire tax (about 60/40) will return.
His rate math: $1M salary in Texas is about **39.4%** (37% plus Medicare) vs **23.8%** on capital gains; in California about 54% vs 37.1%.
Harris cites Tim Dillon on the All-In election stream: the focus shifts from income to assets and equity.
Proposed fix: tax margin loans above a threshold (for example **$10 million**), since borrowing against stock defers tax until death.
Harris says he's an AOC fan but that Ossoff makes more sense for 2028; Calacanis says he would support AOC as president but not necessarily vote for her.
themes.watch: Calacanis says he has used margin loans himself, including to buy a ranch.

takeaways.title: Map data-center exposure by state: Texas, Georgia and Ohio hold 40%+ of planned capacity.
Track whether Texas passes the tax, power, water and union-labor package Baker described.
Budget corporate AI seats at $100-300 a month and audit usage, not flat plans.
Watch publisher licensing deals as the sign of how training-data cases settle.
Model high-tax-state scenarios, including a margin-loan tax above $10M.

claims.claim: Democrats make peace with data-center builders, who agree to pay for power and taxes.
Texas passes laws requiring new data centers to pay taxes, hold power prices, protect water and use union labor.
Slowing the data-center trade pushes the US into a recession of two to four years.
OpenAI targets $600 billion of total compute spend.
Corporate AI subscriptions rise to $100-300 per seat per month.
New York and California top tax rates reach 60%.
The failed billionaire tax returns and passes next time.
